item.title: Judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit seeking to block Alaska Senate certification if GOP loses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, two days before Election Day. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote that the relief the government sought was “infeasible” because many ballots have already been cast and mixed together, the AP reported . She also wrote that the government “provides no workable plan” for separating ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan and investigating them “in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy.” Gleason found the federal government did not have the ability to bring the case, NPR reported . Justice Department attorneys are expected to appeal, according to NPR. The ruling does not end the criminal investigation into how the second Sullivan got on the ballot. It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department sued last month in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Oct. 28, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity. "I'm not naïve," he said. In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law. "Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections." Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2002, wrote in a statement that the people of her state deserve a full explanation. "Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments," she wrote. "By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong." Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. "Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation." Rep. James Comer, the Republican head of the House Oversight Committee, said Oct. 29 that the committee is "taking action" to launch an investigation into the matter, including an inquiry into whether any crimes may have been committed. ABC News also reported Oct. 29 that the DOJ had issued a wave of new subpoenas as it probes whether the alleged recruitment scheme may have run afoul of federal conspiracy laws. On Friday, Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for Alaska, confirmed there is a criminal investigation, saying it had been underway for months. He said the Times report led to a "significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, but declined to say what crimes are being examined and said he was "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed," according to CBS News . Before the ruling, the Justice Department had also asked Gleason to order state officials to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan" so it could investigate possible voter confusion, and it requested action before Monday . State attorneys had asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the ballot already distinguishes the two men. It lists the senator as Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican and the incumbent, and the challenger as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party, the AP reported . In a filing Saturday, Alaska's Republican-run government urged Gleason to dismiss the case, calling it a "meritless lawsuit" and the ballot request "both disturbing and impossible" because it couldn't be carried out without violating voter privacy, the AP reported . "Not every wrong can be righted in federal court," the state wrote. The Trump administration says it is trying to combat fraud. On Friday, a federal appeals court rejected a similar DOJ request in California to set aside disputed ballots. An FBI agent also visited the Petersburg business of a Sullivan donor to ask whether he had been misled, the AP reported . The donor said he hadn't. "Everybody knows who the incumbent is," he said. At a rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., on Friday, Trump said Peltola "should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted," adding that Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision, MS NOW reported . No one has been charged. Peltola said at a rally in Anchorage that she was "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." Asked whether someone on her campaign could have been involved, she told KTUU, "I honestly have no idea." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement, and Dan J. Sullivan has long denied running at Democrats' behest. On CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Sen. Sullivan said he doubted Peltola’s denials. “There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” he said. Asked about certification, he said, “I’m going to accept the results of the election.” Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who leads the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that criminal charges might make sense. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent of Vermont, said on CBS’ “Face the Nation” that what Democrats did “seems to me to be pretty dumb,” adding, “It’s not illegal.” Dunleavy, the Republican governor, suggested his state investigation could still affect the outcome. “If we find out there’s wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that’s what happens,” he told NewsNation on Friday. The outcome of the fight could still have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a move to block or erase a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to the Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last month. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said last month of the lawsuit. The suit argued that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, also moved to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Oct. 26, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Before Gleason's ruling, many legal experts said the lawsuit had a slim chance of success. First, it required a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts said, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters did not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? Voters decide the race Tuesday. The Justice Department is expected to appeal Gleason’s ruling, while the federal criminal investigation, Dunleavy’s state investigation and the House Oversight Committee’s inquiry continue. An appeal would likely only matter in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." item.title: Pete Hegseth is facing a new threat — and it's not just from Democrats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Earlier this year, Senate Republicans decided to tighten the screws on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The Pentagon had, for months, stonewalled lawmakers' request for materials related to the military's deadly targeting of alleged drug traffickers in Latin America. So this spring, the GOP-led Senate Armed Services Committee made a threat: grant access to the documents or it would block one of the Trump administration's political nominees. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Hegseth relented, said two people familiar with the exchange, speaking like some others on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations and the secretary's standing with Congress. Spokespeople for the committee and the Pentagon declined to address questions about the episode. The standoff, which has not been previously reported, illustrates Hegseth's increasing susceptibility to congressional oversight and how he might attempt to navigate a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill should Democrats prevail in this week's midterm elections. With limited exception, Republican lawmakers have declined to stand in Hegseth's way while he has purged dozens of senior military leaders he's deemed disloyal, waged an eight-month war in Iran without the consent of Congress and pursued an unprecedented campaign against the illicit drug trade. Democrats would give Hegseth far less room for maneuver once the next Congress convenes in January. Already, some are threatening to investigate and try to remove him from office if they reclaim a majority. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement that, "despite threats of sham witch hunts," Hegseth is "100% committed" to leading the Defense Department "until the end" of President Donald Trump's term and to advancing the president's agenda for the military. The secretary "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Parnell said, adding that the department under Hegseth "has followed the law." Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in an interview that, as chairman, he would probe three areas: military operations, politicization of the armed forces and potential corruption in the Pentagon's awarding of defense contracts. The Defense Department is readying for such inquires. Those preparations include accounting for the likelihood that if Democrats take charge they will summon military officers to testify on Capitol Hill, people familiar with the matter said. Hegseth faces a more imminent challenge, though. When lawmakers return to Washington later this month, the House will probably vote on an effort to impeach him over the Iran war. That effort is being led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie (Kentucky), a frequent critic of the administration. "There's a decent chance that it could pass the House, and I think that would be a stain on his record," Massie said in an interview. "If he's contemplating leaving, this would be a good time to do it." The House vote is expected to be close, but the effort is highly unlikely to result in a conviction if it advances to the Senate for a trial. Some officials in the administration and in Congress have mused recently that Hegseth may leave the Pentagon if Republicans lose heavily in the midterms - either to avoid congressional scrutiny or to pursue potential political ambitions. It's possible, too, that the president could remove Hegseth if voters punish the GOP over the Iran war, though Trump has said he stands by him. Two people familiar with Hegseth's thinking said the secretary wants to stay in office for four years. One said it's "silly" to think Democrats having greater control on Capitol Hill will change that. The other person said that Hegseth's September address to hundreds of service members in Quantico, Virginia, was meant to be a road map for his next two years in office, including priorities such as building a new U.S. military base and adopting advanced weaponry. An impeachment would be difficult for Hegseth if he does not stay in office, with significant legal costs and less control over what the Defense Department provides to congressional investigators, another person said. Asked by a reporter Thursday about the prospect of an impeachment, Trump - twice impeached himself - called the threat against Hegseth "terrible" and repeated his confidence in the secretary. "He's a great warrior," the president said. Some Democrats acknowledged being concerned that, should they regain a majority in Congress, repeatedly targeting Hegseth could imperil their ability to compromise with Republicans on critical defense legislation. Still, many of those who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon say that Hegseth hasn't worked with them for his two years in office. "Since I became ranking member, I have had the cellphone number of every single secretary of defense," said Smith, who has held the prominent House role for nearly 16 years. "Hegseth does not speak to me." Others in the party have vowed to oust Hegseth. Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colorado), told reporters in October that he would do "everything possible" to remove Hegseth if Democrats retake the House. Hegseth's defenders say they loathe the thought of Trump giving the Democrats "a scalp" by forcing him out, one administration official said. With the president's support, Hegseth has survived multiple controversies, including his use of the commercial messaging app Signal to share highly sensitive details on an imminent military strike and the military's decision to kill two people who survived a strike on an alleged drug boat. But in recent weeks, members of both parties have grown more willing to confront Hegseth, signaling they will block his preferred choices to lead the Army and denouncing his call to live-stream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who committed a mass killing at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. Current and former officials familiar with the Pentagon's standing on Capitol Hill said that Hegseth's challenge after the midterms will be to shore up bipartisan support for the military and defend his record as lawmakers from both parties have grown more critical of him. Two of the officials asserted that Hegseth could work across party lines, depending on how aggressive Democrats were in their investigations. Still, several others predicted that his critics, both in Congress and in the Pentagon, could feel more emboldened to oppose him if Democrats take power. "Pete has made so many enemies - and uncontrollable enemies," one person familiar said. item.title: Which party has a better chance of winning the midterms? What the latest polls say.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are just three days away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is running out — and the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is reaching its final form — and some clear polling trends have emerged. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.7 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.2 points on the generic ballot. Three days later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But with three days to go, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.5 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 6.5 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . New polls from CNN and Data for Progress show Jackson ahead by 4 points and 5 points, respectively. Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Twelve polls have been conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 7 percentage points . New surveys from CBS Detroit and CNN both give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. A new Activote poll shows a statistical tie; a new Suffolk University poll shows Brown leading by 3. Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . A new Echelon Insights survey gives Ossoff a 15-point lead . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 11 points, on average . One of the most recent nonpartisan surveys showed him ahead by 14 . New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month. Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . Some September polls showed a tie, or Sullivan slightly ahead. Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . A new Echelon Insights poll gives Turek a 2-point lead; a new co/efficient poll shows Hinson ahead by the same amount. Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins were small — between 2 and 6 points. But the Democrat seems to be closing strong: a new YouGov Blue poll gives Talarico an 8-point lead ; a new CNN survey shows him ahead by 6 ; and a new Activote poll has him edging Paxton by 4 . A Quantus Insights survey released on Friday gives Paxton a 1-point advantage . Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Ricketts ahead by 1 point; a New York Times/Siena University survey released on Saturday gives Ricketts a 6-point lead. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say : Only one survey conducted over the last month shows Marshall ahead (by a single point). The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). A new CNN poll has Hamilton up by 4 ; a new Emerson College survey puts him ahead by roughly the same amount . On Friday, the Washington Post released a poll showing Hamilton lapping Marshall by about 10 points. But the paper questioned its own results , noting that Republicans responded at much lower rates than Democrats. South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham held a narrow lead in most fall surveys . But it was small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Friday gave Andrews a 5-point advantage; a new New York Times/Siena University poll shows the two candidates essentially tied. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59.9% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37.3% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -22.6% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. item.title: At 11th hour, Dem Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Mich. Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary , Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. “Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living. “At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: “None of this matters." Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker . Democrats had hoped that Sunday would be a show of unity. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded. The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, faces Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term. Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals. After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.” Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support. Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for the nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters. “We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement. The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.” “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Hertel wrote, and won't let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers. “This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post. Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’ Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began. Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats , said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. “I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.” Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions resurfaced, complicating efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, in the primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition. How did we get here? The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women. Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his August win. Last week Stevens’ fiancé told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.” El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.” He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.” Trump and Republicans revel in the discord Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.” “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!” A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said in a statement that Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers. “When Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who ran against Abdul El-Sayed and knows him better than anyone, stands with Mike Rogers, Michigan should take notice,” he said. ___ Cappelletti reported from Washington. item.title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but the stock market's sweetest stretch might be now
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed. The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October. Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn’t happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Yahoo Finance Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off. "I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are." Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June. History is on the buyers' side From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%. Yahoo Finance The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample. Chips just sprang a possible bear trap The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year. On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses. Chip stocks briefly broke below their July low Friday, then closed back above it. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close. The case for waiting Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart. BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held. So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Pineapple express brings potentially historic flooding to Southwest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An atmospheric river referred to as the "pineapple express" is bringing heavy rain to parts of the Desert Southwest and Southern California over Halloween weekend, just over a week after destructive flooding plagued parts of Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah. These atmospheric rivers often fuel heavy rain events in the West, especially in a stronger El Niño winter. We'll discuss more about this pattern after laying out the important forecast details through this weekend. New: Mandatory evacuations are ongoing in parts of Sedona, Arizona near Oak Creek, as well as parts of Archuleta County, near Pagosa Springs, Colorado. The San Juan River is forecast to crest as high as 19 feet tonight, breaking historic records. ( COMPLETE COVERAGE: Super El Niño of 2026-27 ) When and where will these soakings arrive? A large batch of precipitation is ramping up and spreading further into the West as Sunday progresses. An area of low pressure charged by this atmospheric river will move onshore and spread its heavy rain across the West. The heaviest rain is the red locations on the map below. While Phoenix just misses this region, it is still in the level 2 of 4 threat on this map. Flagstaff, Arizona; Zion National Park, Utah and pockets of northern New Mexico and southern Colorado could see the greatest rainfall and rainfall rates. What are the potential impacts? A more serious flash flood threat is in play for the Desert Southwest this weekend, but there will be some concern for wintry weather, too. Below are the current flood and winter weather alerts. The ground is still saturated from the 2 to 5 inches of rain that soaked the area last week, triggering major flash flooding in northern Arizona , New Mexico, southern Colorado and southern Utah . The map below shows total rainfall in the Southwest. Areas shaded in darker green and yellow could see more dangerous, widespread flash flooding. The areas of greatest concern are: Elevations below snow level in southwestern Colorado and the immediate Four Corners area The Phoenix metro's north and east sides and the Mogollon Rim of northern Arizona The canyonlands of southern Utah Any ground scorched by recent wildfires, which is particularly susceptible to producing fast-moving debris flows, rock and mudslides, even in modest rainfall. According to the National Weather Service in Flagstaff, Arizona, rivers such as the Little Colorado and Verde, could run high for days after this weekend's latest soaking. If you had weekend plans to do any hiking in the parks of southern Utah, southern Colorado and Arizona, you should consider canceling. Fast-moving, life-threatening flash floods can sweep rapidly through slot canyons. Over the higher elevations, this precipitation may fall as snow over the higher peaks of the Rockies and Sierra. This may lead to slippery travel mainly Sunday into Monday over mountain passes. Record moisture for Halloween weekend? What's fueling this soaking is a southward plunge of the jet stream near the West Coast. That jet stream will pull a ribbon of deep tropical moisture called an atmospheric river into the Southwest. This particular atmospheric river tap is originating from near Hawaii, something meteorologists nickname the "pineapple express." Weather map graphic showing a low pressure system and storm arrow approaching the California coast, labeled "Halloween weekend, Oct. 31 - Nov. 1" It's not a strong version of either an atmospheric river or pineapple express, but the moisture fueling this heavy rain could be record-setting for this time of year. According to the National Weather Service, the total moisture in the atmosphere over parts of Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and Utah could be 2 to 3 times the average for the end of October, near record amounts for Halloween weekend. This could be a harbinger, given the tendency for a wetter Southwest during most stronger El Niños from fall through spring. item.title: Shootings across 5 states leave 6 dead and at least 36 injured over Halloween weekend
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Dozens of people were injured and at least six people died in mass shootings as gun violence broke out at nightlife districts in half a dozen cities across the country over the Halloween weekend. Police in Dallas, the site of the deadliest violence, said four people are dead and 15 others were injured following a handful of shootings in the city's Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music, restaurants and nightlife in the city. Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts this weekend. Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators are still trying to determine if the shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related. Comeaux said three separate shootings occurred, and it wasn't immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved. “This is a really big scene. It's spread out,” Comeaux said. “We are interviewing some individuals right now that we have arrested, still trying to figure out exactly how it ties into all the shootings out here.” The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured. One shooting happened after an HBCU football game In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting just outside Legion Field after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, police said. Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game, but the shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue. He said he was “very grateful that more people weren’t injured.” The circumstances of the shooting were unclear. Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and “multiple weapons” had been found and secured. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday's game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division. The Magic City Classic has such a deep history that Alabama State coach Eddie Robinson Jr., a former NFL linebacker and alumnus of the school, proposed creating a Hall of Fame for the game. In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment, police said early Sunday. No updates on their condition were available as of Sunday afternoon. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city's Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said. A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries that were not life-threatening, but it was unclear from a statement by the city's police department and McLean County Coroner’s Office if those people had gunshot wounds. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. Two mass shootings occurred in Arkansas A shooting early Sunday near a strip mall southwest of Little Rock, Arkansas, left one man dead and “several more” injured, city police said on Facebook. Police didn't specify the exact number of injured. And in Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting that happened early Sunday. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting. Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan. Police said a shooting inside a store at an indoor shopping mall in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon at a Spirit Halloween. Another man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said. ___ Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporters Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, contributed to this report.
